notes: Dev ABox revision whose edited relation carries transitivity. belongs_to_language_group (staged: transitive, asymmetric, inverse includes_language) holds between a language and each group it sits in (branch, family). The grammar topic already treats language classification as part of its scope (the main split's inserts classify Scots, Gothic and Hittite). The edit moves Hungarian from the Uralic family into the Slavic branch of Indo-European; families are disjoint, so the Uralic membership goes with it. Related near: the inverse (the Slavic languages now include Hungarian); its stored negative is backed by Wikipedia's 'unrelated to any neighbouring language'. Related far: transitivity through the old branch, 'Is Hungarian a Uralic language?' (yes before; no after, since Hungarian was Uralic only through Finno-Ugric). The first version asked whether Hungarian is Indo-European; all four models answered 'yes' in the 2026-11-12 audit (they do not hold that Hungarian is outside Indo-European), so it was replaced by a question whose stored answer they hold. Derived (revised after review): transitivity through a different bridge than related far (Slavic within Balto-Slavic), a composition that looks up a stored fact about the new branch itself (its proto-language, Proto-Slavic), and a binding through the endonym 'Magyar', a genuinely different name. The direct, paraphrase, cross-lingual and binding questions ask the branch level explicitly ('at the level of Germanic or Romance'), since belongs_to_language_group is many-valued and transitive and an unqualified 'which group' would also be answered fairly by Indo-European or Balto-Slavic after the edit. Unrelated near asks Finnish, Hungarian's best-known relative; an edit that drags the family along would answer Slavic there. Counts are exact-phrase counts in Dolma (v4_dolma-v1_7_llama) except those marked approximate. 2026-11-13 audit fix: related far changed from 'Is Hungarian a Uralic language?' (Llama and Mistral answered no) to 'Is Hungarian distantly related to Finnish?', whose stored yes comes from Wikipedia's Hungary article; bridge: Finnish is Uralic (new check).
